newsitem.title: UK: Clinton has hands tied over foreign policy - IISS.
newsitem.headline: Clinton has hands tied over foreign policy - IISS.

text.p: Domestic affairs and the lack of an obvious security threat will continue to restrict U.S. President Bill Clinton's foreign policy options despite his reelection last year, a leading European think-tank said on Thursday.
"It is as true as ever that if the United States does not lead, very little is done globally," the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in its Strategic Survey for 1996/7.
"But President Clinton's ability to lead is constrained both by challenges to his influence from the Republican Congress and by the lack of a concrete security threat."
The IISS said domestic politics had dominated the 1996 U.S. presidential election race to an extent not seen for many years and Clinton would still have to tread carefully.

"Should he take actions against the electorate's wishes, his position would weaken and his influence would ebb. Congress, particularly when in the grip of the opposition...would rush to fill the developing power vacuum," the report said.

But Clinton also needed to ensure links with Europe did not worsen over U.S. moves -- introduced during the election race in a bid to gather ethnic votes -- to punish foreign companies doing business with "rogue states" such as Cuba, Libya and Iran.
This infuriated Canada and the European Union, which threatened to retaliate.

"Transatlantic divisions over rogue states and global foreign policy threaten the very cohesion of the Atlantic alliance when that cohesion is no longer ensured by a common threat," the IISS report said.

"As a result, and since there is little sign that the problem will soon disappear, the chances that these differences will continue to be an irritant to transatlantic relations -- or perhaps even worse -- are considerable."
But despite the increasing parochialism of politics, the experience of two generations of Cold War leadership meant the U.S. political system thrived on engagement in the world.

"The task of Clinton's second term will be to define that engagement and leadership in terms self-interested enough to sustain U.S. public support, and yet soft-spoken enough to reassure the world that its leadership is not a prelude to U.S. dominance," the IISS said.
The IISS survey concluded that major powers were rapidly losing interest in foreign and security affairs as they became more obsessed with domestic politics.
"Unless (Clinton), and other leaders, look beyond the quotidian tasks, however, the predilection for parochial behaviour will triumph," it said.
"What the events of 1996 overwhelmingly showed was that no state, including the U.S., was immune from foreign meddling in domestic affairs or domestic meddling in foreign affairs.
"The distinction between foreign and domestic is indeed becoming thin and the net result is more incoherence."
